*362. SHRI ANIL SHARMA:† 
SHRI SURYABHAN PATIL VAHADANE: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
refer to answer to Unstarred Question 705, given in the Rajya Sabha on 27th 
July, 2001 and state: 
(a) the details of the shortcomings found by the Group constituted by 
teh High Level Committee, in the functioning of the Institution of Mechanical 
Engineers (India), Mumbai; 
(b) on which date three month's temporary suspension of the Institution 
came into effect; and 
(c) the details of the norms laid for permanent recognition of the 
Instituions like the Institution of Mechanical Engineers (India), Mumbai? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. 
MURLIMANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) The shortcomings found in the functioning of the Institution of 
Mechanical Engineers (India), Mumbai by the Group constituted by the High 
Level Committee are given in statement I (See below). 
† The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Anil 
Sharma.

RAJYA SABHA [ 17 August, 2001] 
(b) The date of effect of the tempor ary suspension of the examinations 
being conducted by the Institution of Mechanical Engineers (India), Mumbai 
came into effect from 23.5.2001, the date of issue of notification. 
(c) The recognition is granted on case to case basis by the High Level 
Committee after examining the comments offered by the All India Council for 
Technical Education. If required the opinion of expert groups formed by the 
High Level Committee is also obtained. Recognition of qualifications are subject 
to review by the High Level Committee. 
Statement-I 
Shortcomings found by the Group formed by the High Level Committee 
are as follows: 
(i) The Institution of Mechanical Engineers (India), Mumbai i.e. IME 
is being operated in an ad-hoc manner. No records of all activities 
are maintained. 
(ii) The management of IME is not along accepted norms. 
(iii) The IME could not provide documents to convince the Committee 
that curriculum meetings were held at regular intervals and that 
the revision of curriculum ever took place. 
(iv) IME appears to be reluctant to give full details of the names, 
qualifications and affiliations of all examiners. It appears that these 
appointments are done in an ad-hoc fashion. There are no 
Committee meeting minutes to suppor t the appointments. In fact ' 
IME has itself stated that they have  no records of qualifications of 
Examiners. Records sh ow that some individuals have been 
examiners/paper-setters for severa l (twenty plus) diverse subjects. 
Like-wise some individuals have examined hundreds of projects. 
Some examiners do not appear to be degree holders in Mechanical 
Engineering. 
(v) Coaching classes are closely asso ciated with IME—this is plain 
from the fact that Governing Council has gone on record to thank 
them. There is no evidence of any contact programmes. 
(vi) A few individuals have extensively travelled abroad on IME 
funds—incurring excessive expenses for short visits. There are no 
records on the outcome/benefits of these visits.

later upon a promise by IME to reform its systems but this does not

(viii) Wim a very poor passing percentage IME seems to have benefited 
a miniscule percentage (around 1 %) of registered candidates and 
most of the others have contributed their valuable earnings to the 
huge cash reserves and assets of IME.

Funds to States under National Agriculture Insurance Scheme 
*363. SHRI GANDHI AZAD: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the State Governments are implementing New agriculture 
Policy-2000; and 
(b) if so, how many States have availed of funds on account of National 
Agriculture Insurance Scheme? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): (a) and (b)A Statement is laid on the Table of 
the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) The first ever National Agriculture Policy was announed in July, 2000. 
Various Central Sector and Centrally Sponsored Schemes are being implemented 
by the Government of India and the State Governments for development of 
agriculture and allied activities as envisaged in the Agriculture Policy. Several 
major initiatives have been taken in th e recent past to accelerate the pace of 
development and implement the objectives of the National Agriculture Policy, 
such as introduction of the Macro Management Scheme, preparation of common 
guidelines for Watershed Development Programmes, creation of Watershed 
Development Fund with a corpus of Rs. 200 crore, launching of a Technology 
Mission for the Integrated Development of Horticulture in North Eastern States, 
introduction of a Scheme for seed crop  insurance, establishment of a Seed 
Bank, measures for increasing the availability of farm credit, introduction of a 
subsidy linked credit scheme for construction/modernization and expansion of 
cold storages and storages for horticulture produce, expansion of the corpus of 
the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund, launching of a Market Information 
Network and promotion of value addition in agriculture through excise 
exemption and other interventions.

(b) National Agriculture Insurance Scheme (NAIS) or 'Rashtriya Krishi 
BimaYojna' was introduced from 1999-2000 Rabi season by the Government of 
India with a view to enlarging coverage in terms of farmers, crops and risks. 
Under the scheme, funds are released to the Implementing Agency, i.e. General 
Insurance Corporation of India, who settle the indemnity claims based on the 
yield data received from the State/UT Governments. These claims are shared 
between the Central Government and State Government on 50:50 basis. At 
present, the scheme is being implemented by 18 States and 2 Union Territories.

Observatory in Laddakh 
*364. SHRI B. J. PANDA: Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) what is the project cost of the observatory in village Hanel in Laddakh 
and by when it is going to be completed; 
(b) what are the main features of this observatory; 
(c) whether there is any scheme to expand the observatory; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof, includin g cost estimates and time schedule 
for completion of the project? 
THE MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND  TECHNOLOGY (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (d) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
18 

[17 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Statement 
Indian Institute of Astrophysics has established a state-of-the-art and 
world's highest astronomical observatory with a 2-meter class optical/infrared 
telescope at Hanle, South-Eastem Laddakh. The cost of the project for setting 
up the high altitude astronomical observa tory is Rs. 38.49 crores. The setting 
up of the Observatory has been completed. The telescope has already received 
its first astronomical image on the night intervening 26/27 September, 2000. 
The main features of th e Observatory are: (i) the site at Hanle has good 
accessibility round the year; (ii) me telescope, its four focal plane instruments, 
and the dome are remotely controlled from Hosakote, Near Bangalore, through 
a dedicated satellite communication link in the INSAT series of satellites, 
making it the first remotely operated astronomical observatory in the country; 
(iii) the telescope incorporates the latest technological developments in the 
field of telescope fabrication. Most importantly, the instrument is a new 
advanced technology telescope and inco rporates short focal ratio (f/1.75 
primary mirror; f/9 Cassegrain), ultra-low expansion mirror and is able to 
withstand the low temperatures in Hanle (-30 degrees Centigrade), and provide 
high image quality, superb pointing and tracking accuracy. 
A proposal for setting up of a Himalayan Binocular Telescope at Mt. 
Saraswati, Hanle, Laddakh has been initiated for inclusion in the Tenth Five 
Year Plan at an estimated cost of approximately Rs. 150 crores.

the ironies of our nation's scientific capability and scientific development is 
that often, we have the state-of-the-art research and scientific capability in the 
country but, at the same time, we have  often demonstrated lack of ability to 
translate that scientific knowledge into benefits for the masses. For example, we 
are one of the few nations that have the capability of having launched satellites 
into space. And yet, even in the 21st Century, we have one of the lowest

the country or they are just contributing to observatories, which are nothing 
but white elephants. In this context, I would like the hon. Minister to let us 
know the main objectives of such observatories. Will they address to issues

DR. MURLIMANOHAR JOSHI: Sir, the issues raised by the hon. Member

know — you are yourself a scientist — that this is the picture of 'Crab Nebula'

the first photograph taken by this instrument which is used to explore the

fundamental researches. Nevertheless, the Co2 monitoring is done in Hanel. 
And for green house gas, one of the stations in the world is in Hanel. So, these 
are also the problems which it will attend to. But, the major part of tliis is to act

Comprehensive Seed Policy 
*373. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to bring before Parliament a 
comprehensive seed policy or to overhaul the existing Seeds Act, 1966; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH): (a) and (b) The 
Government propose to bring forward a comprehensive seed policy and overhaul 
the existing Seeds Act, 1966. This is necessitated by far-reaching changes that 
have taken place in the national economic and agriculture scenario and in the 
international environment since the enactment of the ex isting seeds legislation. 
Moreover special thrust is proposed to be given to production of good quality seed 
in order to meet the food production targets of the future. 
27 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2001] 
The salient features of the proposed seed policy are given below:— 
Varietal Development and Plant Variety Protection 
— An effective sui generis system for intellectual property protection will 
be implemented to stimulate investment in research and development of 
new plant varieties and to facilitate the growth of th> Seed Industry in 
the country. 
Seed production 
—  Steps will be taken to ensure availability of good quality seed in adequate 
quantity. 
—  The 'Seed Village Scheme' will be promoted to facilitate production and 
timely availability of seed of desired crop/ varieties at the local level. Seed 
production will be extended to areas , which are outside the traditional 
seed growing areas.   ' - 
—  Seed Banks will be established for stocking specified quantities of seed of 
required crop/variety for ensuring timely and adequate supply of seeds to 
fanners during adverse conditions. 
Quality Assurance 
—  The Seed Act, 2001 will regulate the sale, import and export of seeds and 
supply of quality seeds to farmers throughout the country. 
—  National Seed Board (NSB) will be established in place of existing Central 
Seed Committee (CSC) and Central Seed Certification Board (CSCB). The 
NSB will have permanent existence with the responsibility of executing 
and implementing the provisions of the Seeds Act and advising the 
Government on all matters relating to seed planning and development etc. The 
Board will function as the apex body in the seed sector. 
Seed distribution and marketing 
—  Private Seed Sector will be encouraged and motivated to restructure and 
reorient their activities for catering to nontraditional areas. 
—  Distribution and marketing of seed of any variety for the purpose of sowing 
and planting will be allowed only if the said variety has been registered by 
the National Seeds Board. National Seed Board may direct a dealer to sell or 
distribute seeds in a specified manner if it is considered necessary to the 
public interest. 
28 

[17 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Infrastructure facilities 
—  Seed processing, storage facilities will be augmented. 
—  Training facilities will be established and a computerized national seed 
grid will be created. 
Transgenic Plant Varieties 
—  All genetically engineered crops/varieties will be tested for 
environmental and bio-safety before their commercial release as per the 
regulations and guidelines of the Environment Protection Act (EPA), 
1986. 
—  The transgenic crops/varieties will be tested to determine their agronomic 
value for at least two seasons under the All India Coordinated Project 
Trials of ICAR. 
Import of seeds and planting material 
— All import of seeds and planting materials, etc. will be allowed freely 
subject to requirements of the Plants , Fruits and Seeds (Regulation of 
import into India) Order, 1989 as amended from time to time. 
Export of Seeds 
— Export of seeds and planting materials will be encouraged through 
promotional programmes and steps will be taken to improve their quality 
and competitiveness to meet the required standards. 
Promotion of domestic seed industry 
— Incentives will be provided to domestic seed industry to encourage and 
promote its growth to enable it to produce seeds of high yielding varieties 
and hybrid seeds at a faster pace to meet the challenges of the domestic 
requirement. 
The salient features of the proposed revised Seeds Act are:— 
—  Establishment of National Seeds Board is proposed in the place of Central 
Seed Committee and Central Seed Certification Board. 
—  Seed of any kind or variety for the purpose of sowing or planting will be 
sold in the country only if the said kind or variety has been registered by 
the National Seeds Board as per the criteria prescribed. 
29 

RAJYA SABHA [ 17 August, 2001 ] 
—  The Government will have the right to exclude certain kind or varieties 
from registration to protect public order or public morality or human, 
animal and plant life and health or to avoid serious prejudice to the 
environment. 
—  National Seeds Board will specify minimum standards on germination, 
genetic and physical purity with respect to any seed of a registered kind 
or variety. 
—  The mark or lable on the seed consignment will indicate that such seed 
conforms to the minimum standards, as specified. 
—  For regulating sale of seeds, no person or dealer will be allowed to carry 
on the business of selling or supplying any seed which is not a registered 
kind/variety. 
—  Farmers will be exempted from the requirement to register their kinds or 
varieties. 
—  National Seeds Board or the State Government may accredit individuals 
or organizations to carry out certification, including self-certification on 
fulfillment of criteria prescribed by the Board. 
—  All seed processing units will require to be registered and to maintain 
minimum specifications. 
—  Import of seed for sale shall be permitted only of registered varieties. 
Registration of such varieties shall be granted on the basis of trial 
conducted from minimum period of 3 seasons in India. 
—  Any person intending to import seed or planting material will declare that 
such materials is, or is not, as the case may be, of transgenic character. 
—  Seed or planting material or transgenic nature will have to carry a 
declaration on their lable to this effect.

US Patent for Indian Scientific Breakthrough 
*378. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India has achieved two major scientific breakthroughs, having 
developed a process to grow organs and a low cost simputer and succeeded in

(b) if so, what are the details in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) A statement is laid on the table of the house. 
Statement 
Details of Major Scientific breakthroughs achieved by India 
A doctor while working at the ma ulana Azad Medical College, New 
Delhi developed a surgical technique for regenerating organs in mammals. It 
has been informed by the inventor that stem cells from body tissues like, 
peritoneum and gut, were selected and colonised with the tissue and organ 
systems in the body using specialised surgical technique. It takes about 2 to 3 
months for the formation of an organ. This is a path breaking achievement as 
this technique has the potential of revolutionalising the medical science as 
one can see the possibility of doing away with organ and tissue transplants. 
No donors are required. As the body forms tissues and organs from its own 
cells, there is no problem of acceptance of foreign body, a problem associated 
with transplants. No post-operative treatment by immundsupressant drugs are 
required as needed in transplant surger y. The application was filed in the US 
Patent and Trademark Office on August 29, 1997 and the patent was granted 
on May 8, 2001. 
The Simputer is a low cost portable alternative device to PC by which 
the benefits of IT can reach the common man. This has been designed and 
developed by the scientists of the Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore. It is 
a hand held computing device. The design goal is to make it usable by people 
who may not be literate. The Simputer o ffers conversion of text to speech. It 
can currently read and speak several Indian languages. Thus, use of simple 
icons to be selected and text to speech output in local language are the primary 
33 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2001] 
means of communication. The user is not  expected to be familiar with the 
currently widespread user interface paradigm like windows, slidebars and pull 
down menus. The projected cost of the Simputer is Rs. 9000/- at large volumes. 
It can take Smart Cards and this enables it to be shared by a community. A 
local community such as the village panchayat, the village school, a kiosk, a 
village postman or even a shopkeeper should be able to loan the device to 
individuals for some length of time and then pass it on to others in the 
community. This would reduce the cost per user. Applications in diverse sectors 
such as micro banking, large data collection, agricultural information and as 
school laboratory are possible at an affordable price.

Changes in Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 
†*380. SHRI KRTPAL PARMAR: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT ANF 
FORESTS be pleased to state: 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
36 

[ 17 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) whether it is a fact that developmental activities in Adivasi and tribal 
areas have been adversely affected as a result of implementation of the Forest 
(Conservation) Act, 1980; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and Government's reaction thereto; 
(c) whether Government would consider to make the Act a bit flexible so 
that developmental activities in Adivasi and tribal areas remain unaffected; 
and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (d) Forests provide several usufructs in meeting the sustenance 
and livelihood needs of the tribals including food during lean period. 
Regulation of diversion of forest to non-forestry activity is in the long term 
interest of the tribal and local commun ities. Therefore, Forest (Conservation) 
Act, 1980 helps in safeguarding interests of the Adivasis and tribals rather 
than adversely affecting them. The Act has adequate flexibility to allow the 
activities that are for the welfare of the tribal community without causing 
irreparable damage to the forest eco-system. 
The Act being regulatory and not prohibitory in nature is flexible enough 
to allow important developmental activities on forest lands and as such no 
change or amendment in the Act is contemplated.

2750. SHRIK.M. SAIFULLAH: 
SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRAIAH: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether China is seeking Indian expertise on WTO, to enable it to 
join the WTO by November, 2001; 
(b) if so, whether WTO is crippling domestic farmers and experts have 
pointed out a need for revision of agriculture policy; 
(c) whether India and China have seriou s reservations about the impact 
of WTO on agriculture; 
(d) whether India is in touch with the countries, who oppose the WTO; 
and 
(e) what steps India is considering in this regard? 
THEMLNISTER OF STATE INTHE MINISTRY OFAGRICULTURE (SHRI 
SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): (a) No, Sir. However, in the various bilateral meetings 
between our delegation and the Chinese delegation held in the context of China's 
accession to WTO, the Chinese side ha ve requested for and have also 
acknowledged receiving our support for the early accession of China to WTO. 
(b) India is a founder member of WTO which came into being on 1.1.1995 
as a successor to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade 1947 (GATT), of 
which also India was a founder member. The Agreement on Agriculture (AoA) 
is one of the Uruguay Round of Agreements which India had signed at Marrakesh 
in April, 1994. WTO provides predictable rule based multilateral trading system 
which protects the member countries from  pressures of their stronger trading 
partners. By virtue of being a member of WTO, India is automatically entitled to 
get the Most Favoured Nation and National Treatment for its exports. WTO 
also has a strong Dispute Settlement Mechanism to resolve any dispute between 
members. 
(c) Under the Agreement on Agriculture (AoA) India's domestic policy 
options for agricultural and rural development have not by and larg. been 
constrained. However, the countries who were not earlier giving export 
50 

[ 17 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
subsidies during the base period from 1986—1990 are prohibited from giving 
export subsidies. The developing countries, however, have no reduction 
commitments during the implementation period for the subsidies given to 
reduce the cost of marketing, exports including the international and domestic 
freight and handling cargo. The experience of the implementation of the AoA 
has brought out a number of issues, which deserve re-balancing and have 
already been flagged by India in its comprehensive proposals submitted in 
WTO as a part of the continuing mandated negotiations. The Indian proposals 
aim at protecting its food and livelihood security and for creating opportunities 
for the exports of its agricultural surpluses. 
In so far as China is concerned, while media reports have mentioned 
reservations about the adverse impact of WTO agreement on the agriculture 
sector of China, no official statement about this from the Chinese Government 
has come to the notice of Government. 
(d) and (e)As part of the ongoing negotiations under the WTO Agreement 
on Agriculture, India alongwith many other developing countries have 
highlighted the fact that the anticipated benefits of liberalization in agriculture 
have not materialized for them because of the continuation of trade distorting 
subsidies by many of the developed co untries and have, therefore, demanded 
substantial reductions in trade distorting domestic support, substantial 
reductions in tariffs and elimination of export subsidies by the developed 
countries and sufficient flexibility to th e developing countries to take care of 
these food security and livelihood concerns. In this regard, India besides 
submitting detailed proposals in the areas of market access, domestic support, 
export competition and food security, has also co-sponsored two proposals on 
'Market Access' and 'Export Credits' al ongwith other developing countries. 
While the proposal on 'Market Access' was co-sponsored by India alongwith 
Cuba, Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Honduras, Kenya, Nigeria, Pakistan, 
Sri Lanka, Uganda, Zimbabwe and Haiti, the proposal on Export Credit was 
co-sponsored alongwith Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay, Bolivia, Chile, 
Costa Rica, Guatemala and Malaysia. As  a part of coalition building with 
other developing countries and to garner support for our point of view, the 
Commerce and Industry Minister has written to all the Trade Minister of WTO 
Members of G-77 group of countries with a view to coordinating our positions 
in the context of Doha Ministerial Conference.

Statement I  
Gist of major recommendations contained in the Report of the National 
Expert Committee on Women Prisoners headed by Justice Krishna Iyer 
1. Policy Making and Monitoring 
(a) A National Policy on Custodial Justice to women should be formulated 
and adopted. A draft policy was suggested by the Expert Committee. 
(b) National Authority on Custodial Justice to Women (NACJW) should 
be constituted to overview and monitor the implementation of the National 
Policy. 
(c) One Member of NACJW be designated as the Ombudsman for 
Custodial Institution for Women in India. 
2. Judicial 
(a) State level ACJAW and Ombudsman be also set up. 
(b) Depending on the individual preferences of States, either the 
jurisdiction of Family Court constituted under the Family court Act 1984 be 
extended or the Women's Court should be instituted to dispense justice to 
women. But it should be mandatory fo r the States to create a separate and 
specialized justice dispensing modality to women. 
(c) Nari Bandigriha Adalat in the nature of mobile judicial camps for 
rendering speedy redress to women in custody. 
 
89 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2001] 
3. Legislative 
(a) Article 252 of the Constitution of India should be invoked to get the 
concurrence of two or more States to bring uniform Comprehensive Prison and 
Prisoner Act throughout the country. 
(b) A comprehensive code to cover the administration of all custodial 
institutions should also be formulated. 
 
(c) Critical assessment of the effi cacy and relevance of various 
legislations bearing on women's status in custody and their criminality should 
be undertaken by the Law Commission. 
(d) Appropriate amendment should be made in the IPC, Cr. PC, Prison 
Act, 1894 and Police Act 1861 to reflect the special needs of women in custody. 
(e) The new Mental Health Bill should reflect the specific 
recommendations of the Committee in respect of the custody and treatment of 
non-criminal and criminal lunatic women. 
4. Administrative 
A, Prisons 
(a) A cadre of prison service should be set up. 
(b) There should be enhanced and protected representation of women in 
the prison cadre. 
(c) There should be women DIG at the State HQ preferably from prison 
service to look after the work relating to women prisons. 
 
(d) Women Superintendents of Women prisons should be made fully 
autonomous. 
(e) There should be permanent wardens and matrons. 
(f) Prisoner's Council should be set up in every prison. 
(g) Socio-legal counseling cells should be set up in every prison 
(h) Released Prisoner's Aid Societies should operate in every district. 
(i) Prison amenities for women and their children should be clearly 
identified preferably in a separate volume of the Prison Manual. 
90 

[ 17 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
B. Police 
(a) A cadre of Women Police should be set up. 
(b) It should be mandatory for each Police Station to have seperate lock 
up for women prisoners. 
(c) A model Police Manual should be compiled and this should carry 
indicative standards of minimum space and other facilities and procedures 
applicable to women when in Police custody. 
(d) Women's Assistance Police Unit should be created. 
C. Social Welfare and Mental Health Custodial Institutions 
(a) A manual to guide the management of these institutions should be 
compiled. 
(b) Greater grant of flexibility and tighter inspection and monitor 
mechanism should be devised. 
(c) A national evaluative profile should be attempt to help streamline 
social welfare custodial institutions. 
(d) Judicial camps should be convened in these institutions. 
(e) Socio-legal counseling cells should operate in these institutes. 
(f) Inmates Councils should be set up in these institutions. 
(g) An escort crops with necessary police powers should be developed to 
provide escorting services to these institutions. 
5. Participative structure 
(a) Recognized individuals and groups should have full access to 
custodial institutions alongwith full rights to inspect institutional record and 
interview inmates in confidence. 
(b) Socio-legal cells to be jointly run by law schools and schools of 
social work should be a ttached to every custodia l centre or a cluster of 
centers.

(b) if so, whether poor allocation of funds has resulted in great shortage 
of teachers, especially in primary scho ols, which is the starting point of all 
progress, which significantly contributes towards poverty alleviation; and 
(c) what steps Government propose to adopt so as to fulfil the 
constitutional obligation of providing free and compulsory education for all 
children between the age of 6 and 14? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RE SOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. 
MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (c) The expenditure on education by the 
Central and State Governments as a percentage of Gross Domestic Product 
(GDP) was 4.01 during 1990-91 in 3.49 in 1997-98. According to the Sixth All 
India Educational Survey (1993), 20.12 per cent primary schools in the country 
were having only one teacher and 41.92 per cent had only two teachers. 
Government launched a number of schemes like Operation Blackboard, District 
Primary Education Programme and Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan which inter alia 
provide assistance to State Governments for appointment of additional teachers 
in primary schools. The Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) is also a holistic step to 
achieve the goal of Universalisation of Elementary Education (UEE) through 
a time bound, integrated approach in partnership with States and local bodies 
and the community. It aims to provide relevant and quality elementary 
education to all children in the 6-14 age group by 2010 with a special focus on 
educational needs of girls, Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and other 
children in difficult circumstances.

widows of Vrindavan who do not wish to return to West Bengal; (ii) setting

from the Central Government, Government of Uttar Pradesh, Government of

hire two buildings with a capacity to accommodate 250 widows each in 
Vrindavan. Certain Voluntary organisations are also running Old Age Homes for the 
marginalised women of Vrindavan. With regard to the suggestion made by

suggestion to Government of Uttar Pradesh for comments/advice.

2833. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to bring radical changes governing 
maintenance to be paid to women, estranged from their husbands to ensure 
quick and reasonable relief by making amendment to Hindu Marriage Act, 
1956, Divorce Act of 1955, Parsi Marriage Act and Muslims Marriage Act; 
(b) whether no changes are contemplated in the maintenance provisions 
that apply to Muslim Women; 
(c) if so, whether Government would convene a meeting of top Muslim 
leaders to carry out similar amendment to the 1986 legislation governing 
Muslim Women in view of their great demand; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. 
MURLIMANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (d) As per the information received from 
the Ministry of Home Affairs, the provisions for maintenance have been 
provided in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 in regard to which the 
Government proposes to introduce a Bill in Parliament to amend Section 125 
of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 to remove the ceiling of maintenance 
as also to make an express provision therein for interim maintenance allowance. 
The provisions contained under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 
1973 are common irrespective of their caste, community, religion etc.    ^ 
As per the information supplied by the Legislative Department, that 
Department has taken up the amendments to the Indian Divorce Act, 1869, the 
Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act, 1936, the Special Marriage Act, 1954 and the 
Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 with a view to provide that the application for 
interim maintenance shall be disposed of within sixty days from the date of 
service of notice to the respondent..Action has been initiated to get this Bill 
passed in the Parliament. It may be mentioned that the Muslim Women are 
governed by the provisions of the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on 
Divorce) Act, 1986 which contemplates to protect the rights of Muslim Women

Committee on norms for rail electrification 
2861. SHRI VUAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a Committee has been formed to conduct an indepedent study for 
fixing norms for electrification projects; if so, the terms of reference of this 
Committee; 
143 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2001] 
(b) the reasons necessitating the appointment of such a Committee, the 
procedure presently being followed in electrification projects; and 
(c) by when the report of this Committee is expected to be received? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI O. RAJAGOPAL): (a) Yes, Sir. The Committee will evolve an appropriate 
criteria including norms for sensitivity analysis for taking up electrification 
projects over the next three Plan periods, i.e. upto the year 2016-17. In evolving 
these criteria, the Committee shall take into account the following:— 
(i) The total availability of energy (both electrical and petroleum) in the 
country and its optimum utilization between different sectors, based 
on energy efficiency; 
(ii) The priority that needs to be given for use of electric energy for 
traction purposes by the Indian Ra ilways, taking into account the 
total capital requirement involved; 
(iii) The capabilities of the two trac tion systems to handle longer/heavier 
passenger/freight trains at higher average/ maximum speeds, but 
operating within the operational a nd infrastructural constraints of 
Indian Railways. 
(iv) Cost to the Organisation caused by a redudancy of existing assets/ 
manpower; coupled with associated benefits derived as a result of 
electrification like reliable power s upply over the electrified route, 
impact on environments, etc; and 
(v) The present methodology of worki ng out of the line haul costs, 
suggest improvements and propose the most viable norms including 
fixing a break even point. The Committee shall evaluate the actual 
rate of return achieved on 3 re presentative electrification projects 
(high density, moderate density and low density) completed more 
than 5 years ago and compare this w ith the projected rate of return 
when the project was proposed. 
(b) Considerable progress has been  made in the field of Railway 
Electrification, in the recent past. Time has now come for a comprehensive 
review of the process and also for evolving a clear plan for the future, keeping 
in view all aspects of Railway working as well as environmental factors affecting 
the choice of traction. It has, therefore, been decided to constitute a Committee 
for determining the norms for further electrification over the next three Plan 
periods. 
144 

[17 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
At present, Railway Electrification projects are taken up based on 
financial appraisal of, and Railways operational requirements for, such projects. 
(c) The term of the Committee expires on 20.09.2001. Its Report is likely to 
be submitted thereafter. 
Unmanned railway level crossings in Himachal Pradesh 
2862. SHRI ANIL SHARMA: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleated to 
state: 
(a) the details of unmanned level crossings in Himachal Pradesh; and 
(b) what steps have been taken to pr event accidental deaths on these 
crossings? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI O. RAJAGOPAL): (a) There are 289 unmanned level crossings in 
Himachal Pradesh. Gauge-wise details are as under— 
On broad gauge       = 6 
On narrow gauge     = 283 
(b) Accidents at unmanned level crossings mainly occur due to 
negligence of the road users who fail to observe the rules and stipulations 
contained in the Motor Vehicle Act, 1988. 
The important steps taken by the Government to prevent accidental deaths 
at Unmanned level crossings are listed below:— 
1. On the road approaches, "Stop Boards" are provided on either aide of the 
level crossings at suitable points within the railway boundary to warn the 
road users. 
2. Speed breakers/rumble strips have been provided on road approaches to 
level crossing so that road vehicle drivers reduce their speed. 
3. Whistle Board are provided on rail approach to level crossings for train 
drivers to whistle from the whistle board till such time as the train 
passes the level crossing gate. 
4. Education of road drivers about safety at unmanned level crossings by 
publicity campaings through media like quickies on TV, cinema slides, 
posters, talks on radio, newspaper advertisements and street plays. 
145 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2001] 
5. Chief Secretaries of States have been requested to help in educating 
road users about safety precautions at level crossings and for exercising 
strict checks while issuing driving licences. 
6. Joint Ambush Checks with civil authorities are conducted to nab 
errant road vehicle drivers under the provisions of the Motor Vehicles 
Act, 1988 and the Railways Act, 1989. 
7. Involvement of village Panchayats in the railways public awareness 
programmes. 
8. Putting up level crossing safety pos ters at village Panchayat Offices 
and at retail petrol pumps. 
9. The unmanned level crossings are progressively being manned in a 
phased manner. Although the initial cost of manning of unmanned 
Level Crossing, has to be borne by the Road authority concerned and 
annual operating & maintenance cost is to be borne by the Railway. 
Considering the serious consequen ces of the accidents at unmanned 
Level Crossings, Railway has sanctioned manning of 4 unmanned 
level crossings identified as hazardous, at its own cost. No proposals 
for Manning of other unmanned leve l crossings have been received

Controversial clinical trial conducted in Regional Cancer Centre, 
Thiruvananthapuram 
SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN (Kerala): Sir, I would like to draw 
the attention of this House to a controversial clinical trial conducted by the 
Regional Cancer Centre in collaboratio n with the Johns Hopkins University, 
Baltimore, U.S. It has become a serious controversy receiving international 
media attention that banned drugs are applied on patients in connection with a 
clinical study on oral cancer in  the Regional Cancer Centre, 
Thiruvananthapuram, in collaboration with the Johns Hopkins University of 
the United States. Poor patients in the RCC are alleged to have .been 
subjected to the trial which exposes them to toxicity from drugs which stand 
banned by the Federal Drugs Administration (FDA) in the United States. The 
substance used on the patients was the tetra methyl form of Nor Dihydro 
Gauceretic Acid (NGDA). The M4N developed by the Johns Hopkins 
University  is in the unsafe category of the FDA. 
This act is in total violation of the ethical and moral conventions of 
administering experimental medicines. Even a sanction from the Drugs 
Controller General of India is not obtained. 
The entire episode had a new turn yesterday when the Johns Hopkins 
University, in its press release through website, stated that they have not 
entrusted to any agency the conduct of the study on this medicine and hence 
they have ordered an inquiry. 
Since the matter is getting new dimensions of such a grave nature, 
the intervention of the Government of India becomes inevitable and hence an 
immediate inquiry is to be conducted into this matter. I would just add this, 
Sir.   I understand that an inquiry has already been conducted by the 
174

Heroes of Goa Liberation Struggle 
SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA (West Bengal): Sir. thank you 
very much for giving me this opportunity. Sir, my Special Mention is with 
regard to the history of Goa Liberation Struggle. Sir, I regret drawing the 
attention of this august House and the concerned Ministry of the Government 
of India regarding the utter neglect of important sites of the history of our 
anti-imperialist struggle. The Goa liberation struggle of the fifties has been an 
epoch-making episode in the annals of history of our anti-colonial struggle. 
The renowned leaders, namely, Tridib Kumar Chawdhury, Madhu Limaye, 
Ananta Joshi, Nana Saheb Goray etc. were put behind the Portugese prison, 
Aguada Fort, Goa. Most of them were detained in cell No. 13 of the said jail 
from July 1955 to February 1957. Th e bravery, sacrifice and commitment of 
the leaders were acclaimed by the nation,  and they were accorded a hero's 
reception. At last, Goa was liberated fro m the Portugese colonial rule. In the 
independent Goa, the Aguada Fort jail was converted into a central jail. It is a 
pity on our part that not even a plaque, depicting the history of the struggle, 
could be seen near or inside cell No. 13 or inside the jail. The same cell, 
where the noble freedom fighters we re detained, now accommodates the 
hardcore criminals and drug peddlars. On inquiry, I found that some old 
patriots still assemble once a year to offer homage to the freedom fighters, 
who had sacrificed their lives. 
I demand of the concerned Ministry to appropriately correct the 
situation and raise a monument to commemorate the anti-imperialist struggle 
by inscribing the names of those valiant fighters so that the values of selfless 
sacrifices could be imbibed by the people of this country. Thank you.

Undue delay In the Completion of gauge conversion work of Lumding-
Badarpur-Silchar Section of N.F. Railway 
SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE (Assam): Sir, I would 
refer to a strong apprehension in the minds of public about some unholy 
nexus between the Railway authorities and the powerful road transport lobby, 
which is affecting the progress in completing the work of gauge conversion in 
the Lumding-Badarpur-Silchar Section of the N.F. Railways. Such 
apprehensions gain confirmation from the fact that the contractors, who have 
been given this work of guage conversion by the Railway authorities and the 
road transport owners on National Highway No. 44 are mostly the same 
personnel. The transport lobby is interested to knock out the Railways from 
operating in this area, although, the pub lic, in general, prefer the railway 
journey, because it is less expensive, less time-consuming and more 
passenger-friendly. Therefore, the transp orters are creating hindrance in the 
work of conversion, by adopting 'go slow tactics', in collusion with the 
railway staff, and the work  has been going on at snail's pace for the last so 
many years. There is prolonged delay and late running of trains for no visible 
reasons. All this is done, in active collaboration with the railway officials and 
the operating staff so that the public becomes disgusted while travelling by 
train and give up the mode of travelling by train. I, therefore, plead with the 
Railway Minister to kindly institute a high-level inquiry into the matter so that 
this unholy nexus is put to an end to in the public interest. Thank you.

SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA  REDDY (Andhra Pradesh):

Setting up of a Supreme Court Bench at Chennai and a High Court Bench 
at Coimbatore 
SHRI KA.RA. SUBBIAN (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I make a request for 
setting up a Supreme Court bench at Chennai and a High Court bench at 
Coimbatore. Right to justice is a fundamental right under article 21 of the 
Constitution, as held by the Supreme Court. Claim for establishment of a 
bench of Supreme Court at Chennai has been turned down by the Supreme 
Court. Sir, we see that almost 60 per ce nt of cases filed in the Supreme Court 
are from Punjab, Jammu and Kashmir, Delhi, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and 
Bihar, whereas 30 to 40 per cent cases are from the four Southern States. 
West Bengal, Orissa, Maharashra, Gujarat and North-Eastern States which 
comprise 60 per cent of the total geogra phical area, and also of the total 
population in this country. Supreme Cour t is inaccessible to Southern States 
because it is situated far away, in Delhi.  Further, the cost to litigants is more. 
Train and other expenses are unbearable. We find that as per 2000 SCC, out 
of the cases reported in S.C., the to tal cases from the North are 84; North 
Western States - 49 cases - 58%; East 4 cases - 5%, South - 22 cases - 26%, 
Maharashtra and Gujarat - 9 cases, 10%.  The objection made by the Supreme 
Court is that the establishment of a bench outside Delhi undermines the 
authority and the dignity of the Court.  As far as the authority is concerned, it 
is  not

RAJYA SABHA [17 August. 2001] 
clear. Judgment by judges, whether from South or South East, is binding 
under article 141 of the Constitution. Whet her the Bench is sitting in Delhi or

calibre and independence of the Judges manning the Court. Chennai is 
centrally situated and is ideal for establishment of a bench there. The tradition 
of the Bar of a chartered High Court is more than 125 years of old. 
Establishment of a circuit bench of Madras High Court at Coimbatore is most 
essential to meet the ends of justice and for rendering justice at the door-steps 
of the ligitant public living in Coimbatore, Salem, Namakkal, Erode, Trichy,

estabhlishment of a Supreme Court bench at Chennai and a High Court bench 
at Coimbatore.  Thank you, Sir.

Magasasay Award recognition to Indian National Wisdom 
PROF. (SHRIMATI) BHARATI RAY (West Bengal): Mr. 
Chairman, Sir, I would like to draw the attention of the House to an event of 
unusual national importance. Usually, we discuss the problems of our 
country. We also need to highlight the positive aspects of our country as well, 
like the silent work done by brilliant but relatively unknown people. Rajendra 
Singh has won the Magasasay Award this year. It is a recognition of Indian 
traditional wisdom and needs to be celebrated. Water is going to be the rarest 
commodity in the world including India. Unless we discover a cheap way to 
desalinise seawater, we shall have to  say like Coleridge, "Water, Water 
everywhere, not a drop to drink". The only way of survival is rainwater 
harvesting. This is what Rajendra Singh has reportedly done by adopting two 
strategies. First, he constructed at Alwar in Rajasthan small dams, not in the 
style of big dams constructed with we stern technology, but in the traditional 
indigenous manner. Secondly, he accomplished it neither with money power 
nor with the Government's assistance. He involved the commu iity and built 
awareness among them about the value of  water and about the value of joint 
community work. Consequently, Alwar suffered no drought ; with crops 
growing, forest becoming greener and four dead rivers brought back to life. 
I urge upon the Minister of Water Resources to take note of it and 
extend support to indigenous experiments in other parts of India as well. 
Water needs maximum attention not only of the States but also of the Centre. 
Indigenous methods of rainwater harvesting and community involvement and 
community participation need national support. 
Thank you.

180 

[17 Augufct, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Sir, I am requesting the Government to  erect a statue in the premises of 
Parliament and release a postal stamp in memory of Shri Pingali Venkaiah, 
the creator of our Tricolour. 
Pingali Venkaiah, a Gandhian, the creator of our nation's Tricolour 
that gave enthusiasm, exuberance and patriotism to our countrymen in 
achieving our independence, died in poverty in a small hut in Vijayawada, 
Andhra Pradesh. His only and ultimate dream was to look at the National 
Flag, designed by him, fluttering at the ramparts of the Red Fort. But the most 
pitiable thing is, neither he nor his family members could afford to take him 
to Delhi to see his National Flag flying' from the Red Fort. He died in such a 
pitiable condition. Is this the recognition that we are giving to a great freedom 
fighter? He met Mahatma Gandhi in South Africa and since then had a very 
close association with him. Our beloved leader, Dr. N.T, Rama Rao, had put 
up a statue of this patriot at the Tank Bund, Hyderabad, Andhra Pradesh. 
The most astonishing thing is that the Central Government has 
neither sanctioned any freedom fighter pension nor any other benefit to his 
family members. The result is : The whole family of our great patriot 
disintegrated and little is known about his two sons and a daughter. The only 
known survivor of this family is his daughter. I think she is earning her 
livelihood by selling papads and pickle. I request the Government to 
immediately sanction pension to the fam ily members of the architect of the 
Tricolour and a lesson depicting his history should be introduced in the 
curriculum of the textbooks. I also request the Government to erect a statue in 
the premises of Parliament and release a postal stamp which will be a 
befitting tribute to the great leader. Thank you.

REVIEW OF NATIONAL EDUCATION POLICY, 1966 
PROF. (SHRIMATI) BHARATI RAY (West Bengal): Sir, I move 
the following Resolution:- 
“That this House recommends that the National Education Policy, 
1986 be reviewed." 
Sir, we are facing a crisis in the field of education. It is time, 
therefore, to concentrate on the Education Policy, and more specifically, on 
the implementation of the policy that we have. We had a National Education 
Policy passed by Parliament in 1986. It was modified by Parliament in 1992, 
and we also had an Approved Plan of Action, 1992. The NEP provided for 
"monitoring and review" every five years. A Central Advisory Board of 
Education was envisaged in the NEP "as a body to play a pivotal role in 
reviewing the educational developments, determining the changes required to 
improve the system and monitoring implementation." But today, we have 
come to a point when crucial decisions are being taken without consulting 
Parliament. If reviews have to be made, they have to be transparent. Well-
known scholars and intellectuals from different branches of knowledge have to 
be consulted. Professionals have to be involved to identify the lacunae and 
find out ways and means to rectify them. 
Sir, education is a vast subject. In this short time at my disposal, I 
will mention only a few points. The NEP emphasises on the universal access, 
universal enrolment and universal retention of all children up to 14 years. 
"Education is for all."  But, see, not even illiteracy has been removed, 
241 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2001] 
23 million boys and 36 millions girls are out of school. Crores of rupees are 
spent on various schemes, but there is no monitoring, no evaluation. In fact, 
the bulk of our children enrolled in schools are first generation learners. What 
steps have the Government taken to enable them to develop an understanding 
of their physical and social environm ent? A majority of students live in 
villages. What is the percentage of the total education budget for education in 
rural areas? Most schools do not have drinking water facility. Some do not 
have even a lavatory. Schools are an assemblage for parrots. The curriculum 
needs to be modernised. But how? Not by introducing Jyotir Vigyan or Vedic 
Mathematics? The curriculum should be addressed to the requirements of the 
life-situations of our students. 
Coming to vocational education, in the NPE 1986, it was stated 4hat 
'Voctional education will be a distinct stream, intended to prepare students for 
identified occupations spanning several areas of activity'. Concern was shown 
for women and the disadvantaged sections in the society. What was not 
detailed out in the NPE was how the vocational education was to be imparted; 
which course, at what level, in what form, was to be imparted at which places, 
and for what sections of people? You must see what kind of skills are needed 
in specific areas, what kind of technici ans are needed where,  what the market 
potentials are. Otherwise, how would you ensure that the students who get 
vocational education are employed or become self-employed? Unless jobs are 
assured, or alternatively, there is scope, and demand for products that a self-
employed person can offer, who will go in for vocational education? 
Vocational training should be imparted on practical lines. The education 
policy must spell out the detailed methodology. 
Coming to higher education, the UGC has not done its job at all. 
Now it is reconstituted with members and people, I am sorry to say, who are 
relatively unknown. That is the mildest term I can use, "relatively unknown". 
The NPE says, "Efforts will be made to delve into India's ancient fund of 
knowledge and to relate it to contemporary reality." But see, we are busy 
trying to introduce Vedic Mathematics, it had its place in history, but it has no 
relationship to modern development process. There is a Report given by the 
CAG that the number of international standards of research is decreasing, the 
number of patenting by Indian scholars is going down. Shall we introduce 
astrology and Vedic Mathematics, and impose a burden
